title: Education GiveSpark Thinking Doesn't Have to Wait for Knowledge
author: GiveSpark
summary: Using the chess expertise research of de Groot (1946) and Chase and Simon (1973), the article establishes that expertise is not superior processing power but accumulated knowledge patterns -- chess masters recall board positions not because they have better memories but because they have stored thousands of familiar configurations. This anchors the article's central argument: the knowledge demand of a question is a teacher's design choice, not a fixed property of the topic, and most educators unknowingly set this demand too high. The article does not argue against knowledge; it argues against the assumption that knowledge must always precede thinking -- children arrive with prior experience that thinking can run on. Willingham's principle that 'memory is the residue of thought' drives the practical conclusion: thinking is the process that installs knowledge.
points: * The knowledge demand of a question is a design choice the teacher makes -- not a fixed property of the topic -- which means the same content can be framed as a locked door or as an open invitation requiring only common experience. * Chess master research shows that expertise is stored patterns, not superior processing: masters failed to outperform beginners on random board positions, proving their recall of real positions comes from knowledge, not better memory hardware. * Children arrive with prior knowledge that thinking can run on before formal instruction: a child who has never studied gravity has dropped things, thrown balls, and climbed trees. * Willingham's principle that 'memory is the residue of thought' reverses the traditional sequence: thinking is not the reward granted once knowledge is installed but the process by which knowledge becomes durable. * The demand does not stay low: teachers raise it deliberately as the unit progresses, and what rises is the knowledge that thinking has to draw on.
quotes: What separates them is not the difficulty of the thinking. It is the amount of knowledge you need before you are allowed in.

Every question you ask a child carries a knowledge demand, an amount they must already know before they can begin to think. And that demand is not fixed by the topic. It is set by you, in the wording.
Shown a real game position for a few seconds, masters could reconstruct it almost perfectly from memory. Weaker players could not. On the random boards, their advantage almost vanished.

The first principle in the US National Research Council's landmark synthesis How People Learn: learners come to the classroom with preconceptions about how the world works, built from years of experience.
The knowledge demand of a question is a design choice. Not a fact about the topic. Not a property of the children. A choice you make, every time you write a question.

Willingham's most quoted line: memory is the residue of thought. We remember what we think about. Thinking is the process that installs knowledge, not the reward we hand out once it's safely installed.
The question was never whether to teach knowledge. The question is how much knowledge we choose to require before we invite them into the thinking.
